entries.title: Hardener: an autonomous behavior-review campaign that replaces crucible
entries.brief: Parked by the operator: settle the Tenter/Hardener design and build the campaign that runs a live-substrate module in a sandbox until it converges
entries.body:
## Goal

Replace `crucible`, the hand-run review-and-fix loop, with `Hardener`.
Hardener is an on-demand campaign after loom that runs a live-substrate module in a sandbox, reviews its behavior round after round, and fixes what it finds until the gates are green.
Then retire `crucible/`, which still writes to `_mill/` and runs its rounds through hand-spawned `crucible-reviewer-<effort>` agents.

## Starting point

- The design under `## Design` (DRAFT): `Tenter` is the round loop on `Treadle`, and `Hardener` is `Shed` wrapping `Tenter` with its own Preflight.
  Rounds respawn every time instead of keeping a persistent thread, and a `progress-judge` runs before and after each round.
- `crucible/README.md` is the method Hardener automates.

## Open before Discussion

- What the handoff must carry losslessly besides the finding-recurrence ledger.
- Where the line falls between the Go scaffolding and the LLM's orchestrator role.
- Whether the round agent reuses the `burler` package or only its prompt template.
- How much of the sandbox provisioning lym automates.

## Done when

- `lym` can start a Hardener campaign against a module and run it unattended to convergence or a round cap.
- `crucible/` is deleted, and the design's durable content lives in package docs.

## Notes

- One of the Someday items on `manifest-retire`'s triage list (`hardener`). Landing this entry removes it from that list.

## Design

> **⚠️ DRAFT. This is an early concept sketch, not a settled design.** Unlike the other module docs (which are *Design — not built* but agreed), this one is still being figured out. The shape below captures what a weekend of hand-running the method taught us and the decisions reached so far in discussion; **expect fields, mechanisms, and even the boundary of the module to change.** Do not implement from this doc yet. When the concept firms up this banner comes off and the doc becomes a normal *Design — not built* entry; per the documentation lifecycle it is eventually deleted into the package header + `overview.md` on landing.
>
> **Hand-executed origin:** `crucible` is the method this module would automate — the hand-run version of the same idea, named separately to avoid colliding with this module's own name. This was developed over the last week out of a concrete need: to **run** actual `reed` code hard enough to surface defects a green `go test` never proves. Six hand-orchestrated rounds fixed what many rounds of text-based review could not — it was genuinely *hardening*.
>
> Not required to get `loom` running — `loom` only ever uses text-review (its `Bouncer`+`Burler` review segments), never behavior-review. Kept separate from the `Treadle`/`Shed` work for exactly that reason: nothing here blocks `loom`.

## Naming: two things, not one

Two distinct layers, split out once the shared-engine design (the `internal/treadleengine` and `internal/shedengine` package documentation) was pinned:

- **`Tenter`** — the review-loop alone: `Treadle` (the generic round-loop engine — judge, gate, round-spawn, cap, pause, lock) configured with a live-substrate-driving round-runner and a behavior-review profile, instead of a `burlerengine` round + text-review profile.
  The direct structural sibling of loom's own text-review segments.
  Not separately runnable in isolation the simple way a text-review segment is, because behavior-review needs a live sandbox/worktree lifecycle around it.
- **`Hardener`** — the full, on-demand, autonomous campaign: `Shed` (the generic outer phase-FSM — see `internal/shedengine`'s package documentation) wrapping `Tenter`, plus Hardener's own Preflight (sandbox provisioning, live-suite readiness).
  This is what gets a worktree spawned for it (via `fabric`) and safe-merges back into parent when done, the same lifecycle `loom` uses, just with `Hardener`'s own producer list carrying `Tenter` where `loom`'s list carries its Discussion, Plan and Webster producers.

`Tenter` is a **behavior-based reviewer**: where a text-review segment reads an artifact, `Tenter` **runs** a live-substrate module, reacts to what it observes, and builds bespoke adversarial scenarios to break it. `Hardener` is a separate, on-demand, **post-loom** campaign — not on the `shuttle → burler → shed → loom` spine — meant to harden a live-substrate module (the archetype: `reed` driving real tmux) before merge.

## Why `Tenter` is not a text-review segment

`Tenter` and a text-review segment share the `burler` *round discipline* (see the `internal/burlerengine` package documentation) — A-review → B-fix, no self-grading, commit-per-fix, fix-everything — but they are different reviewers along two axes:

| | text-review segment | `Tenter` |
|---|---|---|
| Mode | **text** — read the artifact | **behavior** — run the module, react, build scenarios |
| Substrate | in-worktree, fast | a **live sandbox repo**; slow, heavy git/go operations |
| Gate | LLM verdict (or a light `command` gate) | **deterministic**: run the smoke suite N× concurrent, zero stray state |
| Cost | cheap, minutes | token- **and** wall-clock-heavy; a single iteration ran 1–2 hours; a campaign, a weekend |
| When | between every phase (on the spine) | **on demand, after loom**, only when `Hardener` is invoked |

A text-review segment's `command` gate lets a code profile *touch* behavior lightly;
`Tenter` is the heavy tier — driving real substrate and hand-rolling crash/rebirth/concurrency scenarios is its whole job.

## `Tenter`'s round-loop — resolved: `Treadle` drives per-round respawn, no persistent thread

**The engine underneath `Tenter` is a general one, not Tenter-specific — see the `internal/treadleengine` package documentation.**
That doc covers the round-runner interface, the judge-maintained handoff (a general improvement, not just Tenter's),
and the process for getting there (`Tenter` itself is built on `Treadle` only once `Treadle` exists).
What follows here is Tenter's own instance of that shared design.

In the hand-run version (see crucible/README.md), **one persistent orchestrator thread** stayed alive across the campaign: it spawned a fresh round agent per round, **independently verified** the round's work (re-ran the gates from cold state on the committed tree — never trusting the round's own "merge-ready" verdict), **accumulated** an understanding of where the module's bugs live, **targeted** each next round agent ("focus on X"), maintained a **handoff** that survived compaction, and asked the operator what to do next.
The targeting + accumulation is what made the reed campaign's rounds succeed where stateless text-review rounds did not — the round agent kept re-discovering the terrain cold otherwise.

**Resolved: no persistent thread.**
Go itself is the orchestrator (`Treadle`);
each round is three fresh, one-shot spawns, not a living session accumulating state in a context window:

1. **`progress-judge`, pre-round.** `Treadle` spawns a fresh one-shot agent that reads the handoff file, decides what to target next, and writes the round's seed prompt (the file the reviewer will read).
   It then terminates — no lingering session.
2. **Reviewer.** `Treadle` spawns the round agent proper, pointed at the prompt the judge just wrote — the same A-review → B-fix, commit-per-fix, no-self-grading round crucible already runs by hand.
   This is the `burler`-shaped worker;
   the *campaign* loop wrapping it is new, the round itself is not.
3. **`progress-judge`, post-round.** `Treadle` spawns a fresh one-shot agent that reads the handoff plus the round's review/fixer-report artifacts, **independently validates the findings** (crucible's non-negotiable rule — three of the reed campaign's seven rounds self-reported "merge-ready" and were wrong each time), rewrites the handoff in place, and decides whether another round is needed or the campaign has converged.

**Naming, fixed:** the pre/post role above is **`progress-judge`**, reusing the term the text-review gate's own description already uses ("run `burler` rounds → `APPROVED`/`stuck` + `progress-judge` + cap") — not "handler."
"Handler" already names a different thing in loom's existing vocabulary (the A-review→B-fix round worker itself, i.e. the "Reviewer" above) — reusing it for the targeting/validating role would collide with that.

The handoff file is the sole accumulation vehicle;
there is no live memory anywhere in the loop.
The one cost this pays versus a text-review segment today: a `progress-judge` spawn on **both** sides of the reviewer, not just post-round — a text-review segment's judge doesn't do this pre-round targeting for Discussion/Plan/Webster today;
those rounds reuse a fixed rubric, not a dynamically retargeted prompt.

### Pre-round targeting

Superseded by the `internal/treadleengine` package documentation — pre-round targeting is designed there as a general capability `Treadle`'s judge can support, exercised by Tenter's profile and simply unused by a text-review profile. See that doc's "Pre-round targeting" section instead of resolving this here.

### The handoff — two-tier memory, and the one crux

- **Handoff** — a **distilled summary**, **edited in place each round** (not appended, so per-round context stays bounded regardless of round count).
  Always read.
  The orchestrator's compressed understanding + what to target next. *(The hand-run instructions already rewrite it in place per round — this discipline is proven, not new.)*
- **Raw reviews + fixer-reports** — complete, authoritative, **read on demand** when the handoff points at something needing detail.
  Reviews inform *targeting*;
  fixer-reports inform *verification*.

The read-set is *instructions + handoff (always) + selective raw files (on demand)* — **not** "all reviews every round," which would reintroduce the O(N) context growth the handoff exists to kill.

**The one crux for going stateless (per-round respawn):** in the hand-run version a *live* thread held some things implicitly — above all "this finding has recurred before."
A respawn has no live memory, so **anything the thread knew implicitly must become explicit in the handoff.**
The prime suspect is the **finding-identity / recurrence ledger** (which findings reappeared in which rounds): if an in-place edit "cleans up" a finding that looks resolved, the recurrence trail can be silently lost and stuck-detection fails quietly.
So: **distill the prose, but keep the key-ledger lossless.**
The migration persistent-thread → respawn is essentially this one audit — find what the live thread knew implicitly and make it explicit.

### Reuse: only `Bouncer` carries over

`Tenter`'s own review-loop is expected to land as a `Shed` segment: a round producer (this module's own equivalent of the shipped `shedadapters: Burler-round producer`, wrapping whatever `Tenter`'s round mechanism turns out to be — not `burlerengine`) paired with an instance of the shipped `Bouncer: the generic review-gate producer`, the same hand-wired shape `loom`'s own review producers use (folk name "perch," see `CLAUDE.md`'s terminology note — this segment is "a perch" in that same loose sense, same shape, different round producer inside it).
Only `Bouncer` is literally reusable code here: `burlerengine`'s own round mechanism is inherently text/diff-specific (Target/Fasit/Rubric over a `shuttle` session editing text), so `Tenter`'s round producer needs its own from-scratch implementation of the same always-`Stuck`-until-approved contract, not a port of `burlerengine`.
This is the second data point (after `loom`'s own review producers) for whether `internal/treadleengine` is ever fully retired — see the shipped `Retire perch` item's own note that its retirement is a separate call, made once `Tenter` lands.

## `Hardener` — the campaign

The operator's role in the hand-run campaign was mostly **gating** — approve, ask for another round — not irreplaceable judgment.
That is front-loadable into the seed instructions ("run until the gates are green or K rounds;
do not ask").
So `Hardener` can run **autonomously, overnight**, with reed + Go handling **auto-compaction** (which, per the insight above, *is* per-round respawn).
Model rotation across rounds (Opus / Fable / Sonnet) stays as a cheap diversity lens — convergence across *different* models is stronger evidence than N passes from one.

`Hardener`'s own worktree-spawn (via `fabric`) and safe-merge-back-to-parent lifecycle is `Shed`'s job (see `internal/shedengine`'s package documentation) — the same `loom`-shared lifecycle described above, with Hardener's own Preflight (below) instead of loom's.

### The sandbox dependency

`Hardener` cannot run against the module's own repo alone — it needs a **live sandbox repo** to do destructive, stateful things (create worktrees, junctions, spawn tmux, tear down) without corrupting the real repo,
and a maintained **live-driving suite** (`tools/sandbox/SANDBOX-<MODULE>-SUITE.md`) as the substrate-exercising vehicle.
Consequences carried from the hand-run method:

- **Deploy-first.**
  The suite runs the **deployed** binary, not the working tree — re-deploy after every source change or you validate a stale binary.
- **The decisive gate is N× concurrent smoke, not a quiet serial pass** — concurrency + CPU saturation is the amplifier that surfaces teardown races and leaked substrate state.
- **Zero stray substrate state at teardown** is itself an invariant under test.
- **Grow the suite with the module** — a bug found live leaves behind both a `//go:build smoke` regression test and, where visual, a suite scenario.

## The likely `lym` shape (open)

`Tenter`'s defining trait — an accumulating, targeting review-loop — is precisely what lym's thesis otherwise *replaces* with Go.
So this probably is **not** "Go takes over the orchestrator."
More likely: **lym provides the deterministic scaffolding** and the **orchestrator brain stays an LLM** —

- **Go / lym owns** (split across `Shed` and `Treadle`): provision/reset the sandbox, deploy the binary, run the slow gates (smoke suite, zero-stray-state), collect + structure results, maintain handoff files (via `internal/state`), the per-round respawn loop, teardown.
- **LLM orch-brain owns** (Tenter's judge, within `Treadle`): read results, accumulate understanding, decide what to target next, write the next round's focused prompt.
- **`burler`-shaped round agent** (see the `internal/burlerengine` package documentation): the A→B worker, spawned per round (drives the sandbox;
  `fix-scope: source`;
  commit-per-fix).

Whether the round agent literally imports the `burler` package or only follows the same `review-prompt-template.md` discipline is an implementation choice for when this is built.

## Dependencies (tentative)

- `internal/treadleengine` package documentation — the generic round-loop engine `Tenter` would configure (as-built;
  module doc deleted per the documentation lifecycle), independent of whether `Tenter`/`Hardener` ever get built.
- `internal/shedengine`'s package documentation — the generic outer phase-FSM `Hardener` configures;
  same independence as above.
- `shuttle` — spawns the round agents and judges `Treadle`/`Tenter` drive.
- `internal/stencil` — fills the round-agent / orchestrator prompt templates (shared with `burler` and the review gate).
- `internal/state` — handoff + round artifacts on disk (the memory that makes respawn work).
- a **sandbox repo + live suite** — a provisioned environment and a maintained asset, not just code.
- `reed` transitively, via shuttle;
  possibly directly for the overnight/autonomous session + auto-compaction.

## Status / open questions

- ~~Persistent thread vs. per-round respawn~~ — resolved: per-round respawn via `Treadle`'s three-step loop (pre-round `progress-judge` → reviewer → post-round `progress-judge`);
  see above.
- ~~Naming: one module or two?~~ — resolved: `Tenter` (review-loop) + `Hardener` (`Shed` + `Tenter`, the campaign);
  see "Naming" above.
- The shared engine designs (round-runner interface, handoff/ledger format, pre-round-targeting mechanics for `Treadle`;
  the outer FSM for `Shed`) live in their own docs — not decided here, independently of whether `Tenter`/`Hardener` themselves ever get scheduled.
- Exactly what the handoff must carry losslessly (key-ledger confirmed;
  what else?).
- The Go-scaffolding / LLM-brain boundary above.
- Whether it reuses the `burler` package or just the prompt template.
- Sandbox provisioning: how much lym automates vs. a pre-existing sandbox repo.
- The treadle judge stencils (`contracts/stencils/treadle/treadle-template-judge-circling.md`, `treadle-template-judge-milestone.md`, `treadle-template-targeting.md`) are kept for Hardener but unmaintained, and are re-derived from the Bouncer judge (`bouncer/bouncer-template-judge.md`) when Hardener is built, so no dead-code sweep removes them (operator decision 2026-10-16, from the stencil intent audit of 2026-10-15).

**This module is post-loom and on-demand;
nothing here blocks the `burler → shed → loom` spine, nor the `Treadle`/`Shed` work, which proceeds independently of whether `Tenter`/`Hardener` are ever scheduled.**

entries.title: Interactive board view: a regenerated HTML file and a phone-friendly README
entries.brief: board.html rendered with README on every write; a VS Code task opens it in the browser; collapsible README for the GitHub app
entries.body:
Operator 2026-10-04: the board needs an interactive view with filters, reachable without typing a lym command each time.

- Rendering (operator, 2026-10-04: mechanical, never an LLM): `board.html` in `_bolt` is a fixed viewer, changed only when the viewer itself changes, with filters on kind, type and area labels, free-text search and expandable bodies.
  It loads a sibling `board-data.js` (`window.BOARD = {…}`), which lym's Go code rewrites from `board.json` on every board write, committed in the same commit as README.md.
  A plain `fetch` of `board.json` does not work: browsers block it for a page opened from `file://`, while a `<script src>` loads.
  A working demo built on today's data was shown to the operator on 2026-10-04 (filters, grouping into Tasks/Bugs/Enhancements, expandable bodies, light and dark).
- Opening: `lym ide` writes a VS Code task "Open board" into each worktree's VS Code config that opens `<hub>/_bolt/board.html` in the default browser, run from `Tasks: Run Task` or a keybinding; lym resolves the path, so nothing is linked into the worktree and `PATTERN-cwd-resolution` holds (it absorbed `PATTERN-hub-containment` in `04aafa88c`).
  With Microsoft's Live Preview extension installed, the task may open it in a VS Code panel instead; VS Code alone shows HTML as source.
  A link from `_lym` was considered and rejected: `_lym` is the pair's weft, the board is hub-level, and file symlinks are not relied on (Windows).
- Phone: the board repo is private, so GitHub Pages needs a paid plan; instead make README.md easier to read in the GitHub app, grouped by type and area with collapsible `<details>` sections per area and per body.
  Built by `board-readme-per-project` (2026-10-28): `README.md` is the root project's file and every project renders to `project-<slug>.md` beside it, research notes first; the collapsible `<details>` sections per area and per body are not built.
  Since then (`af86384e`, 2026-11-01) `README.md` is the Prime project rendered through the same `projectSection` as every other project: each open project shows its own Running, Ready, Tasks, Notes and Done.
  Since `board-no-project-heading` (`d54f5181`, 2026-11-01) a project with open sub-projects puts its own Tasks, Notes and Done under one heading after the sub-projects: `Own entries` for any project.
  Since `board-root-p0` (`a99b3b4d`, 2026-11-01) the root is a project like the others, handle `P0`: it opens with the same heading, renders to its own `project-root.md`, and has its `##` section last in `README.md`; the `## Prime` wrapper and the `No project` heading are gone, and the slug `root` is reserved.
  Since `project-design-link` (`ffb53ae1`, 2026-11-01) a project's body renders to `design-<slug>.md` and the project's facts line links its slug to that file, in `README.md` and in project files alike.
  Since `project-body-in-render` (`9cf88e2a`, 2026-11-04) `project-<slug>.md` also shows the project's body under its brief, with the body's headings shifted so the shallowest sits at level two; `design-<slug>.md` and the link stay, and `README.md`'s project sections stay without the body.
  Since `readme-shows-discussed` (`1bbcc3b1`, 2026-11-03) a row for a discussed entry stacks a `Sketch` link to `decision-<slug>.md` under its slug, in every table of every board file.
  The priority column is headed `Prio` and belongs to Notes tables only.

Builds on `board-model`'s kind and labels.

Operator 2026-10-12: the README's Running section is one list, with no priority groups.


## Was `ide-prime-setup`

Operator 2026-10-04: the prime's `.vscode/` was copied by hand from millhouse (title "LYMHUB", millhouse keys, a mill `launch.json`); lym should seed it instead, and the setup should fit the orchestrator workflow.
Assume no `.vscode/` exists beforehand, or that it may be deleted and re-seeded by lym.

- Window title: `<SHORTNAME>: <name>` from `.lym-shortname`, upper-cased: `LY: prime` for the prime, `LY: <slug>` for pairs (today `internal/vscode/config.go` writes the bare slug).
- Prime folderOpen chain: `reed up` then `reed attach` only; no `reed add claude` (it adds a plain Claude strand the orchestrator workflow does not use).
- Prime tasks run on demand: "lym: beam start" (`lym beam start`, which replaced the removed `lym orch start`: launches or attaches the orchestrator and takes the terminal) and "lym: open board" (opens the board viewer, see `board-viewer`).
- Keybindings: lym writes a `// lym:begin` … `// lym:end` block into the user `keybindings.json`, the way mill writes its `// mill:begin` block (mill holds Alt+Shift+1–6), e.g. Alt+Shift+0 for orch start and Alt+Shift+9 for open board, binding `workbench.action.tasks.runTask` to the task labels.
- No `launch.json`: mill used it to run Python scripts through the debugger; lym is a binary, so tasks are the mechanism.
- Pairs keep their current chains (driven: attach only).


From `reed-view` Discussion (D15, 2026-10-08): `lym ide spawn` rewrites the whole `// lym:begin` … `// lym:end` block in the user `keybindings.json` on every run, for the reed Alt keys; since `ide-seed-workspace-and-keys`, `lym ide seed` writes the same block too.
This note's keys must be added through the same writer, or each spawn or seed wipes them.

entries.title: Weaver: a cold-start implementer beside Webster, with model escalation
entries.brief: A second implementer built on Millhouse Builder: a fresh agent per batch with its own model, escalating the model when an agent fails; Webster stays fork-based
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-10-11)

Webster stays fork-based: its implementer and verify-fix forks start at once with Master's context and run on Master's model.
Weaver is a second implementer beside it, built on Millhouse's "Builder" (skill `mill-go`), that runs a cold-start agent per batch, so each agent can take its own model, and escalates the model when an agent fails.

## Seen (research, 2026-10-11)

- Webster spawns one cold agent today: the recovery strand.
  When a fork reports `stuck` or writes no report twice, Master runs `lym webster recover-batch` (`contracts/stencils/webster/webster-template-master.md`), which starts a fresh shuttle/reed strand with a full cold-start prompt (`internal/websterengine/recoverbatch.go`).
  Its model is `webster.yaml` `recovery` (default `opus[high]`), against `master` at `sonnet[medium]`; that is Webster's only model escalation, and a batch gets at most two recoveries.
- Builder (`plugins/mill/skills/mill-go-base/SKILL.md` in the Millhouse worktree) is a lean orchestrator that never reads cards or diffs.
  Per batch it starts a fresh, non-fork agent with a model from config (`roles.implementer.model`), and the agent reads only its batch file and the overview's Shared Decisions.
  It has no automatic model escalation: a stuck batch gets one fresh retry on the same tier, then a plan edit with a `## Prior failure` note, then a question to the parent.
- Millhouse's cold starts were slow: each agent read much background and loaded its tools before it began work.
  Likely further costs visible in the skill: a review loop per batch, finalize replaying every batch's verify in turn, and a state commit on every status change.

## Shape

Weaver is, in effect, Webster's recovery strand used as the normal path.

- From Webster: the Go bracket verbs (begin-batch, record-batch, recover-batch), the report contract and classification, suspect paths, partition and sequencing, the plan-level verify gate and failure ladder, the shuttle/reed spawn path, and `RenderRecoveryPrompt` with `uncommitted_paths` and the failure digest.
- From Builder: a cold, scoped agent per batch that reads only its cards and Shared Decisions, a model and effort per role per spawn, and a one-shot self-resolve before halting.
- New in neither: an escalation ladder per failed attempt, for example `sonnet` → `opus` → `opus[high]`, set in config.
- Open: how to keep cold-start cost down (a kick-start pack per batch, see `kick-start-pack`), and how a run chooses Weaver over Webster (recipe row or config).

## Idea: Weaver as a Shed run (operator, 2026-10-11)

Loom's driver now does little: most of a loom run is driven mechanically, and the driver acts only when something goes wrong.
Weaver gets the same split: a Weaver run is a Shed-like run in which each batch is a producer, and a Master Weaver drives it the way a driver drives loom, stepping in only when a batch fails.

Open against the code:
- A Shed recipe's rows are fixed, while a plan's batch count is not: either the recipe is generated from the plan, or one batch producer loops over the batch index, as the Burler round loops over rounds.
- The escalation ladder could be Shed rows: a batch's `OnStuck` points at the same batch on the next model tier, and the last tier's `OnStuck` escalates to Master Weaver.
- Whether Master Weaver is an LLM at all on the happy path, or only the escalation target, as the hub orchestrator is for loom.

## Idea: batches formed as the run goes (operator, 2026-10-11)

Batches are not fixed up front.
The run starts from the plan's linear card list, and a batchifier forms the first batches: the cards that can be spawned right now.
Batches, or single cards, whose glyphs do not overlap are spawned in parallel, each in its own worktree.
Each time a batch finishes, the batchifier runs again over the remaining cards and forms the next batch or batches.
The plan is updated as the run goes, since an implementer may have to deviate from it, and the next batchifier pass reads the updated plan.

Open against the code:
- This answers the fixed-rows question above: the run is a frontier of ready batches, not a fixed row list.
  The recipe can still be fixed if the batches are data, not rows: a Batchify row forms the frontier, a Batch-Run row runs it and loops back to Batchify while cards remain, then the run goes on to the plan-level verify, the way the Burler round loops over rounds.
  New for Shed: one row that runs several spawns in parallel and finishes when all of them have.
- Parallel worktrees need a merge back into the task branch after each batch; glyph disjointness rules out textual conflicts but not semantic ones, so the verify gate runs on the merged result.
- Who writes an implementer's deviation into the plan: for glyph renames a Webster fork reports them and Go rewrites the pending cards (dd86d742f), which Weaver may follow; and how the batchifier tells a deviated card's new glyphs from its planned ones.
- What the existing batcher module (`batcher` config) and Webster's partition and sequencing already give a batchifier.

## Was `webster-parallel-execution`

From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday.
Give each DAG-independent group its own `fabric`-spawned worktree, so concurrent cards stop sharing one git index.
A speed optimization over an already-correct sequential system.
The loom plan spec and `internal/websterengine`'s package documentation describe the sequential model it would extend.

## Design

> **Status: parked, not rejected — one shape was rejected, a second is open.** What two explorations rejected is *concurrent forks inside one working tree*, which race on a single shared git index; the 2026-08-20 worktree-per-group shape below does not share that index and is not covered by that rejection. Read past this banner before concluding the idea is dead — the earlier wording said "rejected for now both times" and, until the 2026-08-29 designs audit, sent readers away before the open shape, the measured case study, and the decision gate.
> Still parked, though one of its original three reasons has since fallen: the **Adopt quarry's glyph alphabet as the plan alphabet** item shipped (`go.mod` now requires `github.com/Knatte18/quarry`), so the DAG source this doc used to wait on exists. What still parks it: it is a speed optimization over an already-correct sequential system, and webster's landed card-list rewrite (`internal/websterengine`) should get real running mileage first. Reopen it on the measured evidence the Decision gate section names, never on estimate.
> Per the documentation lifecycle, if this is ever picked up the durable parts fold into `internal/websterengine`'s package doc and this file is deleted; if abandoned, this file is simply deleted.

## Why it's parked

loom-plan-spec.md is deliberately a flat, sequential card list with **no DAG wired into scheduling**.
Running cards as *parallel* forks would require reintroducing a DAG and worktree isolation, which reopens exactly the problem sequential execution avoids: git's index/staging area is a single shared file per working tree, so two forks concurrently committing — even to fully disjoint files — race on the same lock.
Current (2026) ecosystem guidance treats worktree isolation as effectively required for concurrent subagents on the same repo.
A declared-disjoint card pair that turns out (via deviation) to actually overlap is a **live corruption risk** in a concurrent-no-worktree model, not just a bookkeeping problem to fix after the fact as it is sequentially;
quarry would also see other forks' uncommitted, potentially syntactically-broken in-flight edits while serving a concurrent fork's query, since there's no filesystem isolation between them.

**A possible middle ground, if revisited:** let forks edit concurrently (the LLM-thinking-dominated part) but serialize the actual `git add`+commit+verify step through a mutex in webster's Go orchestration ("edit in parallel, land sequentially").
Even this requires *strictly enforced* file-disjointness (not just DAG-edge-absence) to be safe.
Not built.

## A possible unblocking shape (2026-08-20)

A structural alternative to the rejected concurrent-forks-in-one-tree shape above: each DAG-independent group (a batch, possibly one card) gets its own `fabric`-spawned worktree — genuinely its own git index/HEAD, which is what the rejected shape lacked — running the existing `Preflight → Webster → Finalize` row set unchanged, with `Webster`'s `Geometry.PlanDir` (already told, not derived) pointed at the source plan and a new batch-filter selecting the one group to run.
Merge-back reuses `fabric`'s existing merge machinery, not new infrastructure, and a group's completion gates on a build+test of the *merged* result rather than of the group's own worktree in isolation.
The ready set recomputes wave to wave rather than being precomputed upfront, so a group that turns out to depend on another's output is simply not ready yet instead of being mis-scheduled.

This shape is what makes the rejection at the top of this doc specific rather than general: that rejection was about concurrent forks sharing one checkout's git index, which worktree-per-group does not do.

Grouping granularity (one card vs. several) is orthogonal to safety — the original rejection above conflated it with the working-tree-sharing hazard, but genuine worktree-per-lane isolation is what actually matters.
Not yet a plan: the DAG source exists now that the **Adopt quarry's glyph alphabet as the plan alphabet** item has shipped,
but it still needs a writeup reconciling this with the still-open questions elsewhere in this doc (typical-plan wave-width evidence, the batchifier/planner change needed to emit groups).

The per-lane mechanics have since shipped elsewhere: batten's recipe (create, seed, run, teardown as ordinary producers) and its run-id addressing carry N concurrent lane runs side by side, so a lane is a batten-style run whose child seed names a webster-lane recipe — none of that machinery is this item's to build.
What remains genuinely webster's: the wave scheduler (event-driven, recomputing the ready set on each lane's merge-back — never a continuously maintained DAG), the plan group-filter, and a non-forking webster variant.
That last one is the real structural change: today's webster runs forks inside the Master session's own context, which binds execution to one session in one worktree;
a lane needs agents spawned into the lane worktree's own reed session instead, scoped to just that lane's group.

## The case study (from an earlier, more detailed design draft, `websterv2.md`, now retired)

A card-level dependency analysis of the 42-card plan that built webster v1 overturned the naive "linear chain" assumption:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Cards | 42 |
| Batches (sequential) | 9 |
| True card-DAG depth (critical path) | 7 |
| Peak wave width | 10 |
| Cards off the critical path | 83% (35 of 42) |
| Wave widths (1→7) | 10, 9, 7, 7, 6, 2, 1 |

- **The batch DAG over-constrains.**
  Sequential batching's own dependency declarations were largely spurious at card granularity — ~26 cards (waves 1–3) could have run as three parallel waves instead of spread across four sequential batches.
- **File-conflicts barely bind** when the plan is create-then-extend — nearly every file-conflict pair is already dependency-ordered into different waves.
- **The tail is the real ceiling, not dependencies** — a hard funnel near the end of a plan (e.g. final registration → sandbox validation) crashes wave widths regardless of fork budget;
  speedup is front-loaded.
- **Honest speedup estimate: ~2–3× wall-clock**, discounted from a naively-computed 3–5× because a wave's wall-clock is its *slowest* card,
  and the heaviest implementation cards tend to sit on the critical path.
  Two caveats push it down further: semantic edges were *inferred* from card descriptions (real edit-time dependencies only add edges and shrink waves), and 42 cards is an atypically large plan — a routine 5–10-card task has little fan-out headroom and would show a speedup near 1×, dominated by warm-context, not parallelism.

## Decision gate, if ever revisited

Run the card-DAG width analysis across several *real* completed plans, weighted for **typical** task size, not this one outlier.
Wide (fat waves, short critical path, low file-conflict) → an executor might pay off.
Narrow (long critical path, most cards chained, or simply few cards) → parallelism won't materialize;
sequential is the complete correct design, not just the MVP.

## Groundwork first (operator, 2026-10-17)

The groundwork Weaver needs, the batchifier moved inside the implementer and the implementer engine chosen by a setting, is the note `implementer-seam`, built and landed before Weaver itself.

## Decision gate run (2026-10-17)

The width analysis ran on 34 real plans (238 cards, 106 batches): `docs/research/webster/parallel-batches-2026-10-17/`.

- Narrow: the median plan has 6 cards and a critical path of 4, so unlimited worktrees give about 1.6x at best (1.3x counting same-package cards as dependent), with 2 to 3 cards runnable together.
- Webster's actual batches leave about 1.0 to 1.1x, since batching by package already groups dependent cards.
- 14 to 18% of batch pairs disjoint on paper still touched a common file; 16% of changed files were outside the batch's declared targets.
- Shared docs (`doc.go`, `docs/overview.md`, `PATTERN.md`) and `cmd/lym/testdata/test-budget.yaml` serialize most plans; 65% of cards list one of them.
  `test-budget.yaml` is one line per package, so different packages' raises merge cleanly in git unless adjacent; it is a false scheduling dependency.
- A batchifier aiming at parallelism would gain roughly 1.3x to 1.6x on 8 to 17-card plans by ignoring `test-budget.yaml`, moving shared-doc edits to a final card and getting honest per-card file lists; nothing on the about 40% of plans with 4 or fewer cards.

### Operator decision (2026-10-17)

Weaver's batchifier keeps forming clusters of cards from the plan's flat card list that can run in parallel safely enough and efficiently; today's batcher, which groups contiguous cards by cost, cannot serve this, so Weaver gets a new one.
The measure for it is the card-level width (cp and w columns of the study), not the batch level.

### Operator view, not a decision: a DAG batchifier (2026-10-17)

- The plan's card order is not given to be a good or logical order, and today's limit of joining only contiguous cards may not be needed.
- Cards that touch the same glyphs belong in one batch, even with cards between them, as long as no card between them depends on the first and is depended on by the later one.
- Ordering the cards and forming the batches can be done mechanically by a Go program over a DAG.
- A Codex implementer needs Weaver anyway, since Webster's forks are a Claude Code feature.

### Operator view, not a decision: one batch's life (2026-10-18)

For each batch:

1. Create the batch's worktree with `lym fabric`, so it has its own `.lym` and `_lym` folders.
2. Copy the relevant part of the plan into the worktree's `_lym`.
3. Seed the agent's instructions into the worktree; to the cold agent the worktree is an ordinary working folder, and it need not know anything outside it started it.
4. Start a cold agent in the worktree; it does its work, writes a report with any deviations from the plan, and ends.
5. Merge the worktree's work into the parent worktree, resolving conflicts; a good plan leaves little to resolve.
6. Tear the worktree down as usual.

### Orch recommendation on the batch life

- Steps 1 to 4 run for several ready batches at once; step 5 runs one batch at a time under a lock, since the task branch has one head.
- A ready batch's worktree starts from the task branch as it stands when the batch starts, so later batches see earlier merges.
- Before step 5, the batch's own card gate runs in its worktree; after step 5, the verify runs on the merged result; a failure goes up the escalation ladder (a fresh agent on a stronger model in the same worktree, then the arbiter).
- After step 5, the batchifier runs again over the remaining cards, reading the report's deviations, and starts the next ready batches.
- Parallel tests share the hub's gate slots, which caps how many batches verify at once.
- A batch pair is an ordinary pair that pushes to origin like any other (operator, 2026-10-18): its commits are part of the implementation, and an agent continuing the work on another machine must see what a batch left half done.
  An earlier orch recommendation here, that batch pairs stay local-only, was wrong; `batten-start-speed` built that local-only mode from it before the correction, and `fabric-remote-async` has since removed it (`lym fabric add --local` is gone).
  Teardown runs off the critical path, after the merge, so the next batch never waits for it: `lym fabric remove` now returns after its local steps and a detached child pushes the archive tags and deletes the branches on origin.
  The operator saw 10 to 12 s for an add; where is unmeasured, and the loomyard repo's checkout (about 3,150 files) was not timed.

### Orch recommendation on the DAG batchifier

Edges come from the cards' targets and `Uses:`; joining two cards into one batch is legal when it keeps the batch graph acyclic, which is the condition above; a cost budget caps a batch's size; ready batches with no edge between them run in parallel.
The DAG is only as good as the declared targets: the plan spec says `Uses:` completeness cannot be proven at plan time, and 16% of changed files in the study were outside the batch's targets, so the verify on the merged result stays the real gate.

### Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-17)

- Weaver starts cold agents; that is what sets it apart from Webster, which forks.
- A Master Weaver LLM could run several cold agents at once as background processes, one batch per worktree; a Go scheduler could do the same.
- Little is gained from parallel implementers because tasks are already split by the packages they touch: the board's labels and `depends_on` are that parallelism, and work better than expected.
- Weaver is a Go process with an arbiter at hand, not an LLM master.
  Go runs the batchifier after every finished batch and decides which cards suit the next spawns.
  The batchifier is then part of Weaver, not a producer row of its own before the implementer as loom's `Batchifier` row is before `Webster` today; this replaces the Batchify and Batch-Run rows sketched under "batches formed as the run goes".
- A batchifier that does its job leaves few conflicts between batches, and a fast Haiku should resolve the ones left quickly.

### Orch recommendation

If parallel batches are built, a Go scheduler forms, starts, waits for, merges and verifies the batches, and an LLM is called only when a batch fails, as loom's Go driver and arbiter do.
Given the numbers, building it now buys little.
The conflicts the study saw (`wiring.go`, `doc.go`, `refusal-spec.md`) are mostly both sides adding an entry at one spot, which Haiku can merge.
A merge git makes cleanly can still be wrong (one batch changes a signature, the other adds a call to the old one); the verify on the merged result catches it, and a failure there goes up the escalation ladder: a stronger model, then the arbiter.

## The separable, cheap win already taken

A planner that emits true card dependencies (`depends-on`) instead of an over-constrained batch line recovers most of the *width* insight with **no worktrees and no concurrent execution** — this is exactly what loom-plan-spec.md already does.
Only the *executor that actually runs the width* (this entry) remains parked.

## Relationship to quarry (Part B of the retired draft)

The retired `websterv2.md` draft also had a Part B — structured impact lookup via `go/packages`/`gopls` (find-all-references as a Go verb instead of LLM-driven grep).
That idea is superseded, not lost: it's the direct ancestor of [quarry](https://github.com/Knatte18/quarry), which generalizes it to a multi-language, daemon-based design.

## Parallel batch pieces (folded from `parallel-batch-parts`, 2026-11-01)

Webster stays serial (operator, 2026-11-01): a Webster fork inherits its master's working directory and a context full of paths into the task worktree, so keeping it inside another worktree needs hooks and directory flags everywhere and soon turns messy.
Parallel batches belong to Weaver, whose cold agents start in their own worktree.
The pieces they need:

1. A DAG batchifier: edges from the cards' targets and `Uses:`, cards joined into batches while the batch graph stays acyclic and under a cost budget, ready batches chosen.
2. A worktree per batch, created for the batch and removed after it, built on fabric (`lym fabric add --parent`).
3. Merge-back of each batch worktree into the task branch, with a cheap model such as Haiku resolving textual conflicts.
4. The verify on the merged result and its failure ladder, which Webster's verify gate has.
5. The batch brackets and report: `begin-batch`, `record-batch`, the changed-files guard and the report contract, which Webster has.
6. A view of the graph and the batches (`tools/plandag` counts card overlap today).

Claude Code's own worktree isolation for agents has given the operator only trouble before, so the worktrees are lym's, not Claude Code's.

## Related

- `internal/websterengine`'s package documentation — the sequential model this would extend.
- loom-plan-spec.md — already captures the cheap win (`depends-on`).
- [quarry](https://github.com/Knatte18/quarry) — Part B's successor.
- `orch-any-worktree` (landed in dd11ab09f: `lym fabric add --parent` forks a pair from a parent pair) — umbrella tasks need the same create-from-parent-pair, merge-back and teardown primitive as Weaver's per-batch pairs (orch recommendation, 2026-10-18).

entries.title: Ideas to borrow from comparable agent orchestrators (survey, Oct 2026)
entries.body:
Originally imported from issue #671, which no longer exists because the repository was recreated. This entry holds the full text.

This issue collects features from comparable open-source agent orchestrators that LoomYard could borrow later.
I surveyed each project's README, docs and some source through the GitHub API, plus a few vendor docs pages and fresh web searches, in October 2026.
I left out anything LoomYard already has: a deterministic phase engine, glyph-validated plans, independent review with a judge and a bounce budget, warp/weft records in git, per-task worktree pairs, creel, tender, the self-cycling orch, and severity-tagged review findings with BLOCKING verdicts.
Where LoomYard already solves the same problem another way, the bullet says so, since the other project's approach may still hold something to improve.
Each bullet names its source and the LoomYard module it would touch.
Nothing here is a commitment; these are leads to triage.

## Plan validation and concurrency (quarry, Plan-Write, Batchifier, board)

- **Typed scope operations on cards** — [foremerge](https://github.com/naw103/foremerge) (`docs/conflict-detection.md`, `src/conflict.rs`).
  Each declared scope carries an operation: additive (`add`, `extend`, `modify`) or breaking (`replace`, `remove`, `rename`, `migrate`).
  Deterministic rules flag destructive-vs-additive and divergent-rewrite collisions, even when the files do not overlap.
  LoomYard already types its cards (Create/Edit/Delete/Rename/Move), keeps overlapping tasks apart through board labels, and runs the alignment gate before plan writing and before merge.
  Worth comparing: whether foremerge's operation-pair rules catch a collision the board labels and the alignment gate would miss.
- **Symbol leases between concurrent tasks** — [Fusion](https://github.com/Runfusion/Fusion) (`packages/core/src/tasks/symbol-lock-types.ts`, `file-scope-lease.ts`).
  Durable, expiring leases on symbol keys serialize tasks whose claims overlap.
  Ties are broken deterministically by priority, then age, then id.
  LoomYard covers the same need with board labels that keep overlapping tasks from running in parallel, plus the merge conflict resolver.
  Worth comparing: symbol-level granularity versus label-level, and the deterministic tie-break.
  [ORCH](https://github.com/oxgeneral/ORCH) (`src/domain/scope.ts`) does a cruder glob-prefix version.
- **Requirement-to-card traceability gate** — [Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit) `/analyze` (`templates/commands/analyze.md`) and [Kiro](https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/correctness/).
  Spec Kit reports requirement→task coverage % and terminology drift; Kiro links each property test to a requirement and a task.
  For LoomYard: give decision-record decisions IDs and have the Plan-Write gate refuse a plan with an uncovered decision or a card that traces to none.
- **Criterion amendment ledger** — [oh-my-claudecode](https://github.com/Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-claudecode) (`skills/ralph/SKILL.md`, `docs/adr/03664-ralph-prd-criterion-amendment.md`).
  An acceptance criterion can only be relaxed through a recorded amendment that keeps the original text, reason, evidence and authority.
  For LoomYard: webster and the Webster-review judge could refuse a card whose acceptance text changed without such an entry in weft.
- **Blast-radius verdict per glyph** — [tree-sitter-analyzer](https://github.com/aimasteracc/tree-sitter-analyzer).
  Impact analysis returns SAFE/CAUTION/UNSAFE for an edit target.
  For LoomYard: a `quarry impact <glyph>` that Plan review reads, beyond the existing existence check.
  Studied in `docs/research/quarry/tsa-quarry-2026-10-24/report.md` (idea 4): TSA's verdict envelope is not worth borrowing, `internal/impactset` already derives affected tests, and a typed reference query waits on a recorded plan-gate case.
- **Bugfix spec with fail-on-base test** — [Kiro bugfix specs](https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/bugfix-specs/).
  Current / Expected / Unchanged behaviour in WHEN/THEN form, each becoming a test.
  For LoomYard: a bugfix stencil for Discussion-Write, plus a Go gate that the new test fails on the base commit and passes on the tip.

## Review gates (burler, Bouncer, gate)

- **Cross-model external review with rebuttal** — [ralphex](https://github.com/umputun/ralphex) (README "Custom External Review", `pkg/config/defaults/prompts/codex.txt`).
  Any script that prints `file:line - issue` or `NO ISSUES FOUND` can review the diff.
  Claude fixes each finding or argues against it, and the rebuttal goes into the next round.
  Round 1 reviews the full branch diff; later rounds review only the fixes.
  For LoomYard: a non-Claude reviewer as a second shuttle engine inside a review segment, for independence across model families.
- **Stalemate detection** — ralphex `--review-patience=N`.
  It stops after N rounds that produce no commit and no tree change.
  For LoomYard: the Bouncer could halt a segment before it exhausts its bounce budget.
- **Review verdict bound to content** — [Fusion](https://github.com/Runfusion/Fusion) (`docs/workflow-steps.md` "Content-binding review proof", `packages/core/src/planner/plan-approval.ts`).
  An approval records a fingerprint of the plan or diff, and merge refuses a stale or unprovable approval.
  For LoomYard: stamp each Bouncer verdict in weft with the warp tree SHA and have Publish/PR-Gate refuse one that no longer matches.
  Check first whether webster's plan fingerprint already covers the plan side.
- **Incremental re-verify and "Outdated" findings** — [Traycer](https://docs.traycer.ai/extension/tasks/verification.md) and Fusion's severity-gated verdicts.
  A re-review checks only earlier findings and marks them resolved or outdated; Fusion forbids new non-blocking findings on a re-review.
  For LoomYard: a cheaper re-review round mode for burler, to cut circling.
- **Quorum of differently-angled judges** — [ccswarm](https://github.com/nwiizo/ccswarm) Sangha (`crates/ccswarm/src/workflow/sangha.rs`).
  N read-only members (planner, reviewer, QA) each emit `APPROVE|REVISE`, and the stage passes on quorum.
  For LoomYard: an optional multi-judge Bouncer for high-risk segments.
  ccswarm itself has not implemented dissent resolution yet.
- **Post-implementation convergence check** — [Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit) `/converge` (`templates/commands/converge.md`).
  It classifies gaps as missing, partial, contradicts or **unrequested**, ignores checkbox claims as evidence, and appends a remediation phase rather than free-form fixes.
  For LoomYard: an "unrequested" lens in Webster review against the decision record, to catch scope creep.
- **Risk tier by changed paths** — [yylo](https://github.com/yylo-dev/yylo) (`src/templates/config/risk-policy.json`).
  Globs over auth, migrations, lockfiles and CI pick the reviewer count and whether the full suite runs.
  For LoomYard: choose a segment's review depth and `lym gate test` scope from the diff.
  yylo has since marked this queue as retired (`docs/lifecycle-simplification-migration.md`), so treat it as an idea only.
- **Pre-existing failure baseline** — oh-my-claudecode `ralph verify --write-baseline`.
  Gates fail only on new failures; baseline failures become warnings.
  For LoomYard: `lym gate test` and the webster verify gate could record a base-commit baseline, so implementers stop chasing failures that were already red.
  Counterpoint: LoomYard holds that main is always green, so a baseline would legitimize a red main, and it costs an extra full suite run before work starts.
- **Typed completion signals** — [Bernstein](https://github.com/sipyourdrink-ltd/bernstein) janitor (`src/bernstein/core/quality/janitor.py`).
  A task declares `path_exists`, `test_passes` or `file_contains`; an LLM judge runs only once those pass.
  For LoomYard: cards could declare done-conditions that `record-batch` checks in Go.

## Engine, recipes and governance (shed, tender, orch, board)

- **Hard token and cost budgets** — Fusion per-task budgets (`docs/settings-reference.md#per-task-token-budget`) and [Conductor](https://github.com/microsoft/conductor) `limits.budget_usd` with `budget_mode: audit|enforce` (`docs/workflow-syntax.md`).
  A soft cap alerts once, and a hard cap pauses with a named reason.
  Conductor recommends running in audit mode first.
  For LoomYard: weft already records token usage per round; shed or tender could enforce a per-run cap, starting in audit mode.
- **Cross-run quarantine** — Bernstein (`src/bernstein/core/security/quarantine.py`).
  A task that fails 3 times across runs is skipped or decomposed, and the entry expires after 7 days; host-resource failures are excused.
  For LoomYard: board plus orch, so the orch stops relaunching a doomed task.
- **Abandon as a terminal state with a closed reason list** — Bernstein (`docs/operations/abandonments.md`).
  `ABANDONED` is distinct from `FAILED`, and dependent tasks cascade to `BLOCKED_BY_ABANDON`.
  For LoomYard: shed's terminal outcomes, board dependencies and `report convergence`.
- **Fork a run from a step with a tree snapshot** — Bernstein (`docs/operations/fork-from-step.md`).
  The worktree is snapshotted to `refs/bernstein/snapshots/<run>/<step>` at each step.
  For LoomYard: `shed goto` moves the cursor but does not restore the warp tree; a per-producer ref would.
- **Warm retry guarded by a workspace hash** — Bernstein (`docs/operations/checkpointed-retries.md`).
  A retry resumes or forks the native session only if the workspace hash has not changed, and otherwise falls back to a cold restart.
  For LoomYard: webster's fork recovery.
- **Per-run pinning of prompts** — Conductor `bundle build`; Bernstein refuses to resume after its spec digest changes.
  For LoomYard: record the stencil digests a run started with in weft and have resume warn on drift, complementing `lym stencil diff`.
- **Evidence reuse by input identity** — yylo (`risk_policy.py` `semantic_reuse_decision`).
  Earlier test or review evidence is reused only if its inputs and prompt identity are unchanged; a changed review prompt reruns only the review.
  For LoomYard: shed resume and the gate after a rework.
- **Recipe validator and non-LLM step types** — Conductor `conductor validate` and its script/set steps.
  It catches unreachable steps, bad route targets and undeclared inputs offline, and script steps route on exit code or stdout JSON.
  For LoomYard: extend the shed recipe validator with reachability and stencil output-name checks; a generic script producer could route on `lym gate test`.
- **Mid-run guidance at the next step boundary** — Conductor `conductor guide --text`.
  For LoomYard: creel injects into a live pane today; this would queue guidance for the next producer's prompt instead.
- **Batched operator questions with recorded assumptions** — Conductor `questions` step and Spec Kit `/clarify`.
  Spec Kit asks at most 5 multiple-choice questions ranked by impact × uncertainty, each with a recommended answer, and logs answers in a dated Clarifications section.
  Conductor records unanswered questions as assumptions.
  For LoomYard: Discussion-Write's ask-the-operator protocol and the decision record.
- **Proactive rate-limit wait** — oh-my-claudecode (`src/features/rate-limit-wait/daemon.ts`).
  It reads the 5h/weekly usage windows and their reset times, then resumes blocked panes when the window resets.
  For LoomYard: tender schedules the resume instead of waiting for `revive`.
  Built by `usage-limit-wake`: the orch watcher reads the reset time, holds the orch's deliveries and wakes it one minute after the reset to run `lym tender revive`; batten sends one usage-limit notice per run.
  Still open: the resume itself stays with the orch running `revive`, and tender schedules nothing.
- **Standing goals and scheduled routines** — ORCH goals (`src/domain/goal.ts`, `seedAutonomousTasks`), [CAO](https://github.com/awslabs/cli-agent-orchestrator) cron flows with a gate script (`docs/flows.md`), and Fusion routines (README only).
  For LoomYard: board plus orch, for periodic triage, dependency bumps or `selfreport` sweeps.

## Worktree lifecycle hooks and safety (fabric, batten, Merge-In)

- **User lifecycle hooks** — [dmux](https://github.com/standardagents/dmux) (`src/utils/hooks.ts`, `context/HOOKS.md`).
  Executable hooks named `worktree_created`, `before_worktree_remove`, `pre_merge`, `post_merge`, `run_test` and others are looked up in a team dir (`.dmux-hooks/`), then a local dir, then a global one.
  They receive the slug, worktree path, branch and target branch as env vars.
  For LoomYard: `fabric add` and batten could run hub-configured hooks after pair creation (copy `.env`, install dependencies) and around Merge-In/landing.
  Today fabric installs only its own post-checkout drift hook.
- **Commit-time reservation guard** — [ntm](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm) (`ntm guards check --staged`).
  A pre-commit hook refuses commits touching files another agent holds.
  For LoomYard: an enforcement point for the glyph leases above.
- **Sensitive-path deny-list before commit** — ccswarm (README "Safety").
  It blocks `.env`, `*.pem`, `id_rsa`, `credentials*` and `secrets.y*ml`.
  For LoomYard: a cheap check in `record-batch` and the fabric commit path.
- **Free a paused task's worktree** — [claude-squad](https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad) (`session/instance.go`).
  Pause commits a dirty tree, removes the worktree and keeps the branch; resume recreates it.
  For LoomYard: tender/hibernate for long-parked runs; the weft sibling makes this harder.

## Agent sessions (reed, shuttle)

- **Status from hooks rather than pane scraping** — [agent-of-empires](https://github.com/agent-of-empires/agent-of-empires) (`src/hooks/status_file.rs`).
  Claude hooks write `running`/`waiting`/`idle` to per-instance sidecar files, and pane reconciliation fills the gaps.
  For LoomYard: shuttle already reads the Stop payload; adding a "waiting for input" sidecar could replace screen heuristics.
  Partly built by `shuttle-hook-signals`: `PostToolUse`, `PreCompact` and `PostCompact` hooks touch an activity stamp file in the run directory, which shuttle reads as `LastActivity`.
  Still open: a "waiting for input" signal and the screen heuristics in readiness and startup handling.
- **Reference status patterns and a paste pitfall** — CAO (`providers/claude_code.py`, `docs/inbox-delivery.md`).
  Regexes cover the spinner, the idle prompt, `↑/↓ to navigate` (an open question), plan approval, the trust and bypass dialogs, and "Newer model available".
  Bracketed paste behaves differently in tmux below and above 3.7.
  For LoomYard: compare against shuttle's startup-gate and readiness handling and creel inject.
- **Context forecasting and rotation for every session** — ntm (`docs/context-forecast.md`, `docs/compaction-recovery.md`).
  It warns at over 70% occupancy with under 15 minutes projected, and re-injects a refresher after "Conversation compacted".
  For LoomYard: the orch watcher's cycle, extended to the long-lived webster Master and the loom driver.
  Compaction is now counted as activity (`shuttle-hook-signals`); occupancy forecasting and the refresher re-injection are not built.
- **Edit-loop detector** — Bernstein (`docs/operations/agent-loop-detection.md`).
  It kills an agent that edits the same file 4 or more times within 5 minutes.
  For LoomYard: reed's watchdog or shuttle.
- **Destructive-command policy as a PreToolUse hook** — ntm (README §5).
  It is injected via `--settings` on every launch and holds even in bypass mode.
  For LoomYard: shuttle launch settings, if the agents' deny lists do not already cover this.
- **Staggered spawns** — ntm spaces launches by learned rate limits (README only, algorithm not read).
  For LoomYard: webster fork pacing and batten fan-out.

## Observability and audit (report, weft)

- **Hash-chained, replay-verifiable run journal** — Bernstein (`docs/operations/deterministic-replay.md`).
  `bernstein replay latest --verify` names the first step that diverges, and an Ed25519 run receipt verifies offline.
  For LoomYard: a hash chain over producer outputs in weft would make an archived `archive/<slug>/<tip>` tag self-verifying.
- **Unverified-completion rate** — Bernstein (`docs/operations/verification-tracking.md`).
  It alerts when more than 30% of completions in a window had no test, gate or signal check.
  For LoomYard: a new `lym report` view.
- **Commit-to-record links via git notes** — [AgentNote](https://github.com/wasabeef/AgentNote).
  It attaches the session record behind each commit as a git note on a dedicated ref, plus a commit trailer.
  For LoomYard: a trailer or note on each warp batch commit pointing at its weft record path, so `git log` on the code leads to the run.
- **Run diff** — ccswarm `run diff <a> <b>`.
  For LoomYard: `lym report` comparing two archived runs' timelines and token use.
- **OpenTelemetry tracing** — Conductor.
  For LoomYard: optional spans per producer, alongside `report timing`.

## UI and notifications (orch, tender, board)

- **Web dashboard and push notifications** — agent-of-empires (`docs/guides/web-dashboard.md`, `docs/push-notifications.md`) and ralphex `--serve` (SSE live output, late-join history).
  agent-of-empires adds tunnel access with a rotating token, a phone QR pairing code, a read-only mode, and Web Push on waiting/error with a cooldown.
  For LoomYard: a read-only view over board, `shed status` and creel, and a push when a run reaches PR-Gate, circling or a halt.
  [ralphex notifications](https://github.com/umputun/ralphex) (Slack, Telegram, webhook, custom script) are a lighter first step.
- **Attention feed with acknowledgement states** — ntm (`docs/attention-feed-contract.md`).
  It is a durable stream of items needing the human, each NEW/SEEN/SNOOZED/ACK/DISMISSED, with cursors.
  For LoomYard: a single "what is waiting on me" list across runs for the operator and the orch.
- **Terminal bell on a waiting gate** — Conductor's fleet TUI.
  For LoomYard: a near-free signal from reed when PR-Gate or a parent review is waiting.

## Spec and discussion review (Discussion-Write, Discussion review, stencils)

- **Requirements-quality checklist** — Spec Kit `/checklist` ("unit tests for English").
  Items tagged Completeness/Clarity/Consistency/Measurability/Gap/Traceability carry IDs, cite requirements, and are answered by the reviewer, never ticked by the writer.
  For LoomYard: an artifact the Discussion-review judge must answer item by item.
- **Fixed analysis categories** — [Kiro Analyze Requirements](https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/analyze-requirements/).
  It checks for inconsistency, ambiguity, functional/non-functional conflicts, unstated assumptions and missing edge cases.
  For LoomYard: name these lenses in the Discussion-review stencil.
- **Versioned constitution fed to reviewers** — Spec Kit `constitution`.
  It carries a semver version, amendment dates and a sync-impact report, and its MUST rules feed every analysis.
  For LoomYard: PATTERN.md is enforced by Go tests; handing its rules to plan and code reviewers as numbered MUSTs is the new part.
- **Glob-scoped steering context** — [Kiro steering](https://kiro.dev/docs/steering/).
  Context files load always, on a `fileMatch` glob, manually, or by description match, and support `#[[file:path:12-28]]` includes.
  For LoomYard: stencils could pull in per-area guidance chosen by the paths of a plan's glyphs.
- **Living spec and critique before execution** — [Augment Intent](https://www.augmentcode.com/intent).
  A Critique specialist reviews the spec for feasibility before implementers start, and the spec updates as work lands.
  LoomYard's Discussion and Plan reviews already cover the critique.
  Intent is closed source and Augment says Critique's checks are "not yet fully documented", so nothing more is verifiable.
